claim: An estimated 76 million people worldwide suffer from glaucoma.
source: For example, an estimated 76 million people worldwide suffer from glaucoma (Allison et al., 2020), a disease involving optic nerve damage, and about 1.8 million people are blind due to age-related macular degeneration, a degenerative disease of the central retina affecting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor cells (Mitchell et al., 2018; GBD 2019 Blindness and Vision Impairment Collaborators and Vision Loss Expert Group of the Global Burden of Disease Study, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Allison et al., 2020.

claim: Glaucoma is a disease involving optic nerve damage.
source: For example, an estimated 76 million people worldwide suffer from glaucoma (Allison et al., 2020), a disease involving optic nerve damage, and about 1.8 million people are blind due to age-related macular degeneration, a degenerative disease of the central retina affecting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor cells (Mitchell et al., 2018; GBD 2019 Blindness and Vision Impairment Collaborators and Vision Loss Expert Group of the Global Burden of Disease Study, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: About 1.8 million people are blind due to age-related macular degeneration.
source: For example, an estimated 76 million people worldwide suffer from glaucoma (Allison et al., 2020), a disease involving optic nerve damage, and about 1.8 million people are blind due to age-related macular degeneration, a degenerative disease of the central retina affecting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor cells (Mitchell et al., 2018; GBD 2019 Blindness and Vision Impairment Collaborators and Vision Loss Expert Group of the Global Burden of Disease Study, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mitchell et al., 2018 and GBD 2019 Blindness and Vision Impairment Collaborators and Vision Loss Expert Group of the Global Burden of Disease Study, 2021.

claim: Age-related macular degeneration is a degenerative disease of the central retina affecting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor cells.
source: For example, an estimated 76 million people worldwide suffer from glaucoma (Allison et al., 2020), a disease involving optic nerve damage, and about 1.8 million people are blind due to age-related macular degeneration, a degenerative disease of the central retina affecting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor cells (Mitchell et al., 2018; GBD 2019 Blindness and Vision Impairment Collaborators and Vision Loss Expert Group of the Global Burden of Disease Study, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: The RetNet database lists 271 genes associated with heritable retinal diseases.
source: For example, the RetNet database (Daiger et al., 2022) lists 271 genes associated with heritable retinal diseases.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Daiger et al., 2022.

claim: Knowledge of the genes underlying eye diseases and disorders is still incomplete.
source: Even though the eye probably represents one of the best studied organs, our knowledge of the genes underlying eye diseases and disorders is still incomplete.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the examples provided in the text.

claim: Linkage analysis in patients with cataract, microcornea, microphthalmia, and iris coloboma identified new genomic loci linked to the diseases, but the disease-causing genes have remained elusive.
source: For example, linkage analysis in patients with cataract, microcornea, microphthalmia, and iris coloboma identified new genomic loci linked to the diseases; however, the disease-causing genes have remained elusive (Wang et al., 2007; Sabir et al., 2010; Abouzeid et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2007; Sabir et al., 2010; Abouzeid et al., 2009.

claim: The Cat-Map database lists several additional cataract-associated loci where the underlying disease-causing gene has not been identified.
source: Similarly, the Cat-Map database (Shiels et al., 2010) lists several additional cataract-associated loci where the underlying disease-causing gene has not been identified.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shiels et al., 2010.

claim: There are thousands of genes that have not been experimentally investigated in detail, leaving many genes where potential eye-related functions remain to be discovered.
source: Furthermore, there are still thousands of genes that have not been experimentally investigated in detail, leaving many genes where potential eye-related functions remain to be discovered.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the general state of genomic research.

claim: Systematic knockouts of 4,364 genes in mouse detected ocular phenotypes for 347 genes, with 75% of them not been known as eye-related before.
source: Indeed, systematic knockouts of 4,364 genes in mouse detected ocular phenotypes for 347 genes, with 75% of them not been known as eye-related before (Moore et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moore et al., 2018.

claim: Vision-related genes as well as genes associated with genetic eye disorders remain to be identified and characterized.
source: This indicates that vision-related genes as well as genes associated with genetic eye disorders remain to be identified and characterized.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the previous statement about systematic knockouts.

claim: Many genes that are linked to human eye diseases are inactivated (lost) in non-human mammals that naturally exhibit poor vision.
source: Interestingly, many genes that are linked to human eye diseases are inactivated (lost) in non-human mammals that naturally exhibit poor vision (Emerling et al., 2017; Sharma and Hiller, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Emerling et al., 2017 and Sharma and Hiller, 2020.

claim: Subterranean mammals such as the blind mole rat, naked mole rat, star-nosed mole, and cape golden mole exhibit gene-inactivating mutations in genes implicated in cataract, retinitis pigmentosa, color or night blindness, or macular degeneration in human.
source: For example, subterranean mammals, such as the blind mole rat, naked mole rat, star-nosed mole, and cape golden mole, exhibit gene-inactivating mutations in genes implicated in cataract, retinitis pigmentosa, color or night blindness, or macular degeneration in human (e.g. ABCA4, BEST1, CRYBA1, EYS, GJA8, GNAT2, PDE6C, ROM1, and SLC24A1) (Sharma and Hiller, 2020; Kim et al., 2011; Fang et al., 2014; Emerling and Springer, 2014; Prudent et al., 2016; Partha et al., 2017; Emerling, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Symptoms that characterize human eye diseases resemble traits found in subterranean mammals, such as highly degenerated retinae and lenses and sometimes blindness.
source: Symptoms that characterize these human eye diseases resemble traits found in these subterranean mammals, such as highly degenerated retinae and lenses and sometimes blindness.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the comparison between human eye diseases and subterranean mammal traits.

claim: Losses of the short wave sensitive opsin (OPN1SW), which is linked to color blindness in humans, occurred in several mammalian lineages such as cetaceans, bats, sloths, and armadillos.
source: Similarly, losses of the short wave sensitive opsin (OPN1SW), which is linked to color blindness in humans, occurred in several mammalian lineages such as cetaceans, bats, sloths, and armadillos that are consequently inferred to have monochromatic vision (Emerling et al., 2017; Meredith et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2009; Emerling and Springer, 2015; Sadier et al., 2018; Springer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Cetaceans, bats, sloths, and armadillos are inferred to have monochromatic vision.
source: Similarly, losses of the short wave sensitive opsin (OPN1SW), which is linked to color blindness in humans, occurred in several mammalian lineages such as cetaceans, bats, sloths, and armadillos that are consequently inferred to have monochromatic vision (Emerling et al., 2017; Meredith et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2009; Emerling and Springer, 2015; Sadier et al., 2018; Springer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the loss of OPN1SW and citations to multiple studies.

claim: Subterranean mammals exhibit widespread sequence and transcription factor binding site divergence in eye-related regulatory elements.
source: In addition to losses of vision-related genes, subterranean mammals also exhibit widespread sequence and transcription factor binding site divergence in eye-related regulatory elements (Roscito et al., 2018; Langer et al., 2018; Langer and Hiller, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Roscito et al., 2018; Langer et al., 2018; Langer and Hiller, 2019.

claim: Mutations in eye-related regulatory elements can cause mis-expression of target genes in ocular tissues such as the lens.
source: Such mutations can cause mis-expression of target genes in ocular tissues such as the lens (Roscito et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Roscito et al., 2021.

claim: Loss and divergence of vision-related genes and regulatory elements in subterranean mammals is likely caused by the lack of natural selection on maintaining functional eyes in a dark environment.
source: Loss and divergence of vision-related genes and regulatory elements in these mammals is likely caused by the lack of natural selection on maintaining functional eyes in a dark environment.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from evolutionary theory and the observed patterns.

claim: Previous studies established a clear association between naturally occurring poor vision phenotypes and regressive evolution of the genetic machinery required for functional eyes.
source: Taken together, previous studies established a clear association between naturally occurring poor vision phenotypes and regressive evolution of the genetic machinery required for functional eyes (Emerling et al., 2017; Partha et al., 2017; Roscito et al., 2018; Langer et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A genome-wide screen was performed for genes preferentially lost in independent mammalian lineages with a low visual acuity.
source: Here, we performed a genome-wide screen for genes preferentially lost in independent mammalian lineages with a low visual acuity with the goal of revealing currently uncharacterized genes, where vision-related gene loss patterns would predict vision-related functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the study's methodology.

claim: The screen revealed previously unknown losses of several functionally uncharacterized genes, among them SERPINE3.
source: In addition to identifying losses of known vision-related genes, our screen revealed previously unknown losses of several functionally uncharacterized genes, among them SERPINE3, which is lost in 18 mammalian lineages that often do not use vision as the primary sense.
evidence: The claim is supported by the results of the genome-wide screen described in the study.

claim: SERPINE3 is lost in 18 mammalian lineages that often do not use vision as the primary sense.
source: In addition to identifying losses of known vision-related genes, our screen revealed previously unknown losses of several functionally uncharacterized genes, among them SERPINE3, which is lost in 18 mammalian lineages that often do not use vision as the primary sense.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data from the extended analysis of 381 additional mammals.

claim: SERPINE3 has the highest expression in eyes of zebrafish and mouse.
source: We show that SERPINE3 has the highest expression in eyes of zebrafish and mouse.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 3A, B, and D.

claim: In the zebrafish retina, serpine3 is expressed in Müller glia cells.
source: In the zebrafish retina, serpine3 is expressed in Müller glia cells, a cell type essential for survival and maintenance of the retina.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 3G and H.

claim: Müller glia cells are essential for survival and maintenance of the retina.
source: In the zebrafish retina, serpine3 is expressed in Müller glia cells, a cell type essential for survival and maintenance of the retina.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about Müller glia cells.

claim: A CRISPR-mediated knockout of serpine3 in zebrafish resulted in alterations in eye shape and defects in retinal layering.
source: A CRISPR-mediated knockout of serpine3 in zebrafish resulted in alterations in eye shape and defects in retinal layering.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4D, E, and F.

claim: Two human polymorphisms that are in linkage with SERPINE3 are associated with eye-related traits.
source: Furthermore, two human polymorphisms that are in linkage with SERPINE3 are associated with eye-related traits.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of GWAS data presented in Figure 4A and discussed in the Results section.

claim: SERPINE3 has a role in vertebrate eyes.
source: Together, these results suggest that SERPINE3 has a role in vertebrate eyes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined evidence from gene loss patterns, expression data, and knockout experiments.

claim: Screens for specific phenotype-associated gene signatures can predict functions of uncharacterized genes.
source: More generally, by integrating comparative genomics with experiments in model organisms, we show that screens for specific phenotype-associated gene signatures can predict functions of uncharacterized genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the successful prediction and validation of SERPINE3's eye-related function.

claim: Visual acuity describes the ability of an animal to resolve static spatial details, which generally reflects how much an animal relies on vision in comparison to other senses.
source: First, visual acuity describes the ability of an animal to resolve static spatial details, which generally reflects how much an animal relies on vision in comparison to other senses (Caves et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Caves et al., 2018 and established knowledge about visual acuity.

claim: Low-acuity species have low visual acuity values <1 (log10(va) <0), which comprises ten species representing seven lineages.
source: Low-acuity species have low visual acuity values <1 (log10(va) <0), which comprises ten species (three echolocating bats, three rodents and four subterranean mammals) representing seven lineages (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the classification scheme used in the study and presented in Figure 1A.

claim: The screen retrieved 29 genes that are preferentially lost in low-acuity species at a false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of 0.05.
source: At a false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of 0.05, our screen retrieved 29 genes, which are preferentially lost in low-acuity species.
evidence: The claim is supported by the results of the Forward Genomics screen presented in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The 29 genes include several known vision-related genes, such as components of the photoreceptor signal transduction cascade (GUCA1B, ARR3), a factor required for retinal organization (CRB1), lens crystallins (CRYBA1, CRYBB3, CRYGS) and the cornea specific keratin 12 (KRT12).
source: These genes include several known vision-related genes, such as components of the photoreceptor signal transduction cascade (GUCA1B, ARR3), a factor required for retinal organization (CRB1), lens crystallins (CRYBA1, CRYBB3, CRYGS) and the cornea specific keratin 12 (KRT12).
evidence: The claim is supported by the list of genes in Figure 1B and established knowledge about their functions.

claim: The set of 29 genes is enriched in vision-related functions such as the Gene Ontology term 'visual perception' (p=1.8e-7), expression in the mouse lens (p=5.5e-3), and human eye diseases (cataract: p=8.5e-3).
source: The set of 29 genes is enriched in vision-related functions such as the Gene Ontology term 'visual perception' (p=1.8e-7), expression in the mouse lens (p=5.5e-3), and human eye diseases (cataract: p=8.5e-3) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by enrichment analysis results presented in Figure 1C.

claim: A control screen for genes that are preferentially lost in high-acuity sister species of the low-acuity mammals retrieved only two genes, none of which have known functions in the eye.
source: To confirm the specificity of these results, we performed a control screen for genes that are preferentially lost in high-acuity sister species of the low-acuity mammals. This control screen retrieved only two genes, none of which have known functions in the eye (Figure 1—source data 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the results of the control screen presented in Figure 1—source data 4.

claim: 15 of the 29 top-ranked hits have no studied role in the eye.
source: Interestingly, while 15 of the 29 top-ranked hits have no studied role in the eye (Figure 1B), many of these genes are expressed in human eyes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the list of genes in Figure 1B and literature review.

claim: RSKR, LACTBL1, LBHD1, and ZNF529 cluster in their expression pattern with other retina phototransduction and visual perception genes.
source: RSKR, LACTBL1, LBHD1, and ZNF529 even cluster in their expression pattern with other retina phototransduction and visual perception genes (Uhlen et al., 2010; Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Uhlen et al., 2010 and data in Figure 1—source data 2.

claim: The preferential loss of these genes in species that exhibit lower visual acuity values predicts an uncharacterized vision-related function for some of these 15 genes.
source: The preferential loss of these genes in species that exhibit lower visual acuity values and that have convergently lost other known vision-related genes predicts an uncharacterized vision-related function for some of these 15 genes (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the gene loss patterns observed in the screen.

claim: SERPINE3 is classified as lost in 7 of the 10 low-acuity mammals.
source: SERPINE3 is largely uncharacterized and classified as lost in 7 of the 10 low-acuity mammals (Figure 1, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—source data 2.

claim: SERPINE3 independently accumulated inactivating mutations in all four subterranean species (cape golden mole, star-nosed mole, naked mole rat, blind mole rat).
source: SERPINE3 independently accumulated inactivating mutations in all four subterranean species (cape golden mole, star-nosed mole, naked mole rat, blind mole rat).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene loss analysis presented in the study.

claim: Within bats, SERPINE3 is inactivated in the two Myotis bats and the big brown bat (Yangochiroptera).
source: Within bats, SERPINE3 is inactivated in the two Myotis bats and the big brown bat (Yangochiroptera).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene loss analysis presented in the study.

claim: The three bat species (two Myotis bats and the big brown bat) use echolocation instead of vision as the primary sense for hunting.
source: These three species use echolocation instead of vision as the primary sense for hunting.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about bat ecology.

claim: Non-echolocating flying foxes (Pteropodidae) that rely more on vision possess an intact SERPINE3 gene.
source: In contrast, non-echolocating flying foxes (Pteropodidae) that rely more on vision, possess an intact SERPINE3 gene.
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene loss analysis presented in the study.

claim: All three modified screens consistently retrieved SERPINE3 as one of the top-ranked hits.
source: All three modified screens consistently retrieved SERPINE3 as one of the top-ranked hits (Figure 1—source data 5 , Figure 1—source data 6, Figure 1—source data 7), showing that this association is robust to the selected thresholds and phenotype definition.
evidence: The claim is supported by the results of the modified screens presented in the supplementary data.

claim: The association between SERPINE3 loss and poor vision is robust to the selected thresholds and phenotype definition.
source: All three modified screens consistently retrieved SERPINE3 as one of the top-ranked hits (Figure 1—source data 5 , Figure 1—source data 6, Figure 1—source data 7), showing that this association is robust to the selected thresholds and phenotype definition.
evidence: The claim is supported by the consistency of results across different screen parameters.

claim: SERPINE3 is inactivated in 70 of the 430 analyzed placental mammals.
source: A detailed analysis of inactivating mutations indicates that SERPINE3 is inactivated in 70 of the 430 analyzed placental mammals and that the gene is convergently lost at least 18 times in placental mammal evolution (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–8).
evidence: The claim is supported by the extended analysis of 381 additional mammalian genomes using TOGA.

claim: SERPINE3 is convergently lost at least 18 times in placental mammal evolution.
source: A detailed analysis of inactivating mutations indicates that SERPINE3 is inactivated in 70 of the 430 analyzed placental mammals and that the gene is convergently lost at least 18 times in placental mammal evolution (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–8).
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis of SERPINE3 losses presented in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: SERPINE3 is lost in several mammalian clades with nocturnal representatives that have a partially burrowing lifestyle such as pangolins (Manidae), aardvark and armadillos (Cingulata).
source: For example, SERPINE3 is lost in several mammalian clades with nocturnal representatives that have a partially burrowing lifestyle such as pangolins (Manidae), aardvark and armadillos (Cingulata), which are characterized by proportionally small eyes (Mittermeier and Wilson, 2011; Myers et al., 2022; Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene loss analysis and citations to Mittermeier and Wilson, 2011; Myers et al., 2022.

claim: Pangolins, aardvark and armadillos are characterized by proportionally small eyes.
source: For example, SERPINE3 is lost in several mammalian clades with nocturnal representatives that have a partially burrowing lifestyle such as pangolins (Manidae), aardvark and armadillos (Cingulata), which are characterized by proportionally small eyes (Mittermeier and Wilson, 2011; Myers et al., 2022; Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mittermeier and Wilson, 2011; Myers et al., 2022.

claim: All representatives of pangolins, aardvark and armadillos use smell and hearing as primary senses for perception of environmental clues and have a poor sense of vision.
source: All representatives of these clades use smell and hearing as primary senses for perception of environmental clues and have a poor sense of vision (DiPaola et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to DiPaola et al., 2020.

claim: SERPINE3 has been lost in the stem lineage of Pilosa (sloths and anteaters).
source: SERPINE3 has also been lost in the stem lineage of Pilosa (sloths and anteaters).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene loss analysis presented in the study.

claim: Extant sloths have rather high visual acuity values (10.2 for southern two-toed sloth).
source: Although extant sloths have rather high visual acuity values (10.2 for southern two-toed sloth) (Veilleux and Kirk, 2014), the Pilosa ancestor was likely a digging/burrowing species (Gaudin and Croft, 2015), indicating that SERPINE3 loss originally occurred in a burrowing species.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Veilleux and Kirk, 2014.

claim: The Pilosa ancestor was likely a digging/burrowing species.
source: Although extant sloths have rather high visual acuity values (10.2 for southern two-toed sloth) (Veilleux and Kirk, 2014), the Pilosa ancestor was likely a digging/burrowing species (Gaudin and Croft, 2015), indicating that SERPINE3 loss originally occurred in a burrowing species.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gaudin and Croft, 2015.

claim: SERPINE3 loss in Pilosa originally occurred in a burrowing species.
source: Although extant sloths have rather high visual acuity values (10.2 for southern two-toed sloth) (Veilleux and Kirk, 2014), the Pilosa ancestor was likely a digging/burrowing species (Gaudin and Croft, 2015), indicating that SERPINE3 loss originally occurred in a burrowing species.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the ancestral lifestyle and the timing of gene loss.

claim: SERPINE3 is lost in solenodon, European shrew and tenrecs (Tenrecidae), species with small eyes that use echolocation for close-range spatial orientation.
source: SERPINE3 is also lost in solenodon, European shrew and tenrecs (Tenrecidae), species with small eyes that use echolocation for close-range spatial orientation (Siemers et al., 2009; Gould, 1965; Eisenberg and Gould, 1966; Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene loss analysis and citations to Siemers et al., 2009; Gould, 1965; Eisenberg and Gould, 1966.

claim: SERPINE3 is convergently lost in seven echolocating bat lineages.
source: For bats, our extended data set shows that SERPINE3 is convergently lost in seven echolocating lineages, but remains intact in all 13 analyzed Pteropodid bats, revealing a clear pattern of convergent losses of this gene restricted to bat lineages relying on laryngeal echolocation (Figure 2—figure supplements 5–7).
evidence: The claim is supported by the extended gene loss analysis in bats presented in Figure 2—figure supplements 5–7.

claim: SERPINE3 remains intact in all 13 analyzed Pteropodid bats.
source: For bats, our extended data set shows that SERPINE3 is convergently lost in seven echolocating lineages, but remains intact in all 13 analyzed Pteropodid bats, revealing a clear pattern of convergent losses of this gene restricted to bat lineages relying on laryngeal echolocation (Figure 2—figure supplements 5–7).
evidence: The claim is supported by the extended gene loss analysis in bats presented in Figure 2—figure supplements 5–7.

claim: There is a clear pattern of convergent losses of SERPINE3 restricted to bat lineages relying on laryngeal echolocation.
source: For bats, our extended data set shows that SERPINE3 is convergently lost in seven echolocating lineages, but remains intact in all 13 analyzed Pteropodid bats, revealing a clear pattern of convergent losses of this gene restricted to bat lineages relying on laryngeal echolocation (Figure 2—figure supplements 5–7).
evidence: The claim is supported by the pattern of gene losses observed in the extended bat analysis.

claim: The sac-winged bat is the only laryngeal echolocating bat with an intact SERPINE3.
source: The sac-winged bat is the only laryngeal echolocating bat with an intact SERPINE3; however, selection rate analysis indicates that the gene evolves under relaxed selection (Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene loss analysis and selection rate analysis presented in Figure 2—source data 4.

claim: SERPINE3 in the sac-winged bat evolves under relaxed selection.
source: The sac-winged bat is the only laryngeal echolocating bat with an intact SERPINE3; however, selection rate analysis indicates that the gene evolves under relaxed selection (Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by selection rate analysis using RELAX presented in Figure 2—source data 4.

claim: SERPINE3 is convergently lost in the fossorial Damara mole rat.
source: Expanding upon the two convergent losses of SERPINE3 in subterranean rodents detected in the initial screen, the gene is also convergently lost in the fossorial Damara mole rat and evolves under relaxed selection in the Transcaucasian mole vole (Figure 2—source data 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 8), while being intact in all other 63 rodents.
evidence: The claim is supported by the extended gene loss analysis in rodents.

claim: SERPINE3 evolves under relaxed selection in the Transcaucasian mole vole.
source: Expanding upon the two convergent losses of SERPINE3 in subterranean rodents detected in the initial screen, the gene is also convergently lost in the fossorial Damara mole rat and evolves under relaxed selection in the Transcaucasian mole vole (Figure 2—source data 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 8), while being intact in all other 63 rodents.
evidence: The claim is supported by selection rate analysis presented in Figure 2—source data 4.

claim: SERPINE3 is intact in all other 63 rodents (excluding those with losses or relaxed selection).
source: Expanding upon the two convergent losses of SERPINE3 in subterranean rodents detected in the initial screen, the gene is also convergently lost in the fossorial Damara mole rat and evolves under relaxed selection in the Transcaucasian mole vole (Figure 2—source data 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 8), while being intact in all other 63 rodents.
evidence: The claim is supported by the extended gene loss analysis in rodents.

claim: SERPINE3 is convergently lost in another clade of fossorial moles (Talpidae) within the order of Eulipotyphla.
source: In the expanded data set, we further uncovered the loss of SERPINE3 in another clade of fossorial moles (Talpidae) within the order of Eulipotyphla (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the extended gene loss analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: A splice site mutation shared between dugong and manatee indicates an ancestral loss of SERPINE3 in the ancestor of sirenians.
source: A splice site mutation shared between dugong and manatee as well as patterns of relaxed selection indicate an ancestral loss of SERPINE3 in the ancestor of sirenians, which mostly use their tactile sense for navigation through murky water (Moore et al., 2021; Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the identification of shared mutations and selection analysis.

claim: Sirenians mostly use their tactile sense for navigation through murky water.
source: A splice site mutation shared between dugong and manatee as well as patterns of relaxed selection indicate an ancestral loss of SERPINE3 in the ancestor of sirenians, which mostly use their tactile sense for navigation through murky water (Moore et al., 2021; Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moore et al., 2021.

claim: The Florida manatee has a reduced ability to resolve spatial detail (va = 1.6) compared to its closest relatives, the African elephant (va = 13.16).
source: Consistent with our definition of poor vision based on visual acuity, the Florida manatee has a reduced ability to resolve spatial detail (va = 1.6, Mass et al., 2012) compared to its closest relatives, the African elephant (va = 13.16, Pettigrew et al., 2010), which has an intact SERPINE3 gene.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mass et al., 2012 and Pettigrew et al., 2010.

claim: The African elephant has an intact SERPINE3 gene.
source: Consistent with our definition of poor vision based on visual acuity, the Florida manatee has a reduced ability to resolve spatial detail (va = 1.6, Mass et al., 2012) compared to its closest relatives, the African elephant (va = 13.16, Pettigrew et al., 2010), which has an intact SERPINE3 gene.
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene loss analysis presented in the study.

claim: SERPINE3 is lost in the cape elephant shrew.
source: Finally, SERPINE3 is also lost in the cape elephant shrew, which is a mostly diurnal species with relatively large eyes (Dengler-Crish et al., 2006); however, loss of SERPINE3 already occurred in the ancestral Afroinsectiphilia lineage (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which was presumably nocturnal (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene loss analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cape elephant shrew is a mostly diurnal species with relatively large eyes.
source: Finally, SERPINE3 is also lost in the cape elephant shrew, which is a mostly diurnal species with relatively large eyes (Dengler-Crish et al., 2006); however, loss of SERPINE3 already occurred in the ancestral Afroinsectiphilia lineage (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which was presumably nocturnal (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dengler-Crish et al., 2006.

claim: Loss of SERPINE3 in the cape elephant shrew already occurred in the ancestral Afroinsectiphilia lineage.
source: Finally, SERPINE3 is also lost in the cape elephant shrew, which is a mostly diurnal species with relatively large eyes (Dengler-Crish et al., 2006); however, loss of SERPINE3 already occurred in the ancestral Afroinsectiphilia lineage (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which was presumably nocturnal (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis of SERPINE3 losses presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ancestral Afroinsectiphilia lineage was presumably nocturnal.
source: Finally, SERPINE3 is also lost in the cape elephant shrew, which is a mostly diurnal species with relatively large eyes (Dengler-Crish et al., 2006); however, loss of SERPINE3 already occurred in the ancestral Afroinsectiphilia lineage (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which was presumably nocturnal (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2017.

claim: Many independent gene losses in species that do not rely on vision as their primary sense predicts a vision-related function for SERPINE3 that became dispensable in these mammals.
source: Together, many independent gene losses in species that do not rely on vision as their primary sense predicts a vision-related function for SERPINE3 that became dispensable in these mammals, leading to convergent SERPINE3 losses due to relaxed selection.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the pattern of convergent gene losses.

claim: Convergent SERPINE3 losses are due to relaxed selection.
source: Together, many independent gene losses in species that do not rely on vision as their primary sense predicts a vision-related function for SERPINE3 that became dispensable in these mammals, leading to convergent SERPINE3 losses due to relaxed selection.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from evolutionary theory and the observed patterns.

claim: SERPINE3 is classified as a member of the serine proteinase inhibitor (SERPIN) family based on sequence homology.
source: Based on sequence homology, SERPINE3 is classified as a member of the serine proteinase inhibitor (SERPIN) family.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and established classification systems.

claim: Many members of the SERPIN family are secreted into the extracellular space and inhibit their substrates by covalent binding.
source: Many members of this family are secreted into the extracellular space and inhibit their substrates by covalent binding (Heit et al., 2013; Law et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Heit et al., 2013 and Law et al., 2006.

claim: Key sequence features of inhibitory serpins are well conserved among placental mammals in SERPINE3.
source: We performed a SERPINE3 sequence analysis, which revealed that key sequence features of inhibitory serpins are well conserved among placental mammals, suggesting that SERPINE3 also functions as a secreted serine proteinase inhibitor (see Material and Methods, Figure 2—figure supplements 9 and 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplements 9 and 10.

claim: SERPINE3 functions as a secreted serine proteinase inhibitor.
source: We performed a SERPINE3 sequence analysis, which revealed that key sequence features of inhibitory serpins are well conserved among placental mammals, suggesting that SERPINE3 also functions as a secreted serine proteinase inhibitor (see Material and Methods, Figure 2—figure supplements 9 and 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from sequence conservation and established knowledge about serpins.

claim: Serpins have roles in coagulation, angiogenesis, neuroprotection and inflammation.
source: Serpins have roles in coagulation, angiogenesis, neuroprotection and inflammation, and several serpins have been implicated in human diseases (Law et al., 2006; Barnstable and Tombran-Tink, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Law et al., 2006 and Barnstable and Tombran-Tink, 2004.

claim: Several serpins have been implicated in human diseases.
source: Serpins have roles in coagulation, angiogenesis, neuroprotection and inflammation, and several serpins have been implicated in human diseases (Law et al., 2006; Barnstable and Tombran-Tink, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Law et al., 2006 and Barnstable and Tombran-Tink, 2004.

claim: The functional role of SERPINE3 is largely unknown as the gene has never been studied in an animal or cellular model.
source: However, the functional role of SERPINE3 is largely unknown as the gene has never been studied in an animal or cellular model.
evidence: The claim is supported by a thorough literature search conducted by the authors.

claim: Serpine3 is upregulated in the mouse retina in response to overexpressing neuroprotective factors.
source: For example, Serpine3 is upregulated in the mouse retina in response to overexpressing neuroprotective factors (Machalińska et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Machalińska et al., 2013.

claim: Serpine3 was upregulated in complement component 3 (C3) knockout mice, which represent a model of the aged retina.
source: Serpine3 was also upregulated in complement component 3 (C3) knockout mice, which represent a model of the aged retina (Rogińska et al., 2017), and downregulated in the eye of knockout mice for Pcare, a causal gene for retinitis pigmentosa (Kevany et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rogińska et al., 2017.

claim: Serpine3 was downregulated in the eye of knockout mice for Pcare, a causal gene for retinitis pigmentosa.
source: Serpine3 was also upregulated in complement component 3 (C3) knockout mice, which represent a model of the aged retina (Rogińska et al., 2017), and downregulated in the eye of knockout mice for Pcare, a causal gene for retinitis pigmentosa (Kevany et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kevany et al., 2015.

claim: Zebrafish has a cone-dominated retina (∼60% cones, ∼40% rods), similar to the central human retina.
source: Zebrafish has proven as valuable model species for the study of eye genetics as it has a cone-dominated retina (∼60% cones, ∼40% rods) (Fadool, 2003), similar to the central human retina.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fadool, 2003 and established knowledge about zebrafish retina.

claim: Zebrafish has a single serpine3 ortholog that is located in a context of conserved gene order.
source: Furthermore, zebrafish have a single serpine3 ortholog that is located in a context of conserved gene order (Figure 4A), which makes zebrafish a suitable model for investigation of serpine3 expression and function.
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis presented in Figure 4A.

claim: RT-qPCR analysis revealed that the highest serpine3 expression is in the eye, followed by expression in the brain.
source: Reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) analysis with two normalization genes (actb and rpl13a with n=8 and n=3 biological replicates, respectively) consistently revealed that the highest serpine3 expression is in the eye, followed by expression in the brain (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Serpine3 expression is significantly higher in eye than in other tissues when normalized to actb.
source: For actb, serpine3 expression is significantly higher in eye than in other tissues (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Serpine3 is specifically expressed in the retina but not in other tissues of the zebrafish eye.
source: Serpine3 is specifically expressed in the retina but not in other tissues of the eye.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data on dissected eye tissues presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Serpine3 expression level is significantly higher in retina without RPE compared to RPE only.
source: The expression level is significantly higher in retina without RPE compared to RPE only (two-sided unequal variances t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Serpine3 expression in RPE only is significantly higher than expression in eye tissue after removing retina and RPE.
source: Although expression in RPE only is low, it is significantly higher than expression in eye tissue after removing retina and RPE (two-sided unequal variances t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Mouse Serpine3 is specifically expressed in the eye but not in colon, cortex, heart, liver, spleen and testis.
source: Similar to zebrafish, mouse Serpine3 expression is highest in whole eye, whereas expression was not detectable in colon, cortex, heart, liver, spleen, and testis (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Chromogenic in situ hybridization shows localized expression of serpine3 in the zebrafish retina, specifically in the inner nuclear layer.
source: Chromogenic in situ hybridization (ISH) shows localized expression of serpine3 (purple) in the retina, specifically in the inner nuclear layer (inlet).
evidence: The claim is supported by ISH data presented in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Fluorescence in situ hybridization shows that serpine3 mRNA expression is localized to cell bodies of Müller glia cells.
source: Fluorescence in situ hybridization shows that serpine3 mRNA expression (yellow) is localized to cell bodies of Müller glia cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data presented in Figure 3G and H.

claim: Serpine3 mRNA is not expressed in bipolar or amacrine cells.
source: Serpine3 mRNA is not expressed in bipolar or amacrine cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data with cell type markers presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is evidence for expression of SERPINE3 in eyes of human, rat, cat, cow and chicken.
source: Despite sparser data, we found evidence for expression of SERPINE3 in eyes of human, rat, cat, cow and chicken, which suggests a conserved expression pattern and a role in vertebrate vision (Figure 3—source data 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of publicly available expression data sets presented in Figure 3—source data 5.

claim: SERPINE3 has a conserved expression pattern in vertebrate eyes.
source: Despite sparser data, we found evidence for expression of SERPINE3 in eyes of human, rat, cat, cow and chicken, which suggests a conserved expression pattern and a role in vertebrate vision (Figure 3—source data 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from expression data across multiple vertebrate species.

claim: Adult homozygous serpine3cbg17 fish were viable and fertile.
source: Adult homozygous serpine3cbg17 fish were viable and fertile.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations of the knockout fish.

claim: The deletion of the transcription start site abolished serpine3 expression in retinae of adult homozygotes for serpine3cbg17 compared to wild type siblings.
source: Using RT-qPCR and ISH, we confirmed that the deletion of the transcription start site abolished serpine3 expression in retinae of adult homozygotes for serpine3cbg17 compared to wild type (WT) siblings (two-sided unequal variances t-test, p=0.049, Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and ISH data presented in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Adult serpine3cbg17 individuals frequently showed notches in the iris of one of the eyes (4 of 5 individuals).
source: We found that adult serpine3cbg17 individuals frequently showed notches in the iris of one of the eyes (4 of 5 individuals, white arrows in Figure 4D, Figure 4—source data 2, source data on Dryad), which affected the eye's overall shape.
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic observations presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Serpine3cbg18 fish showed a high frequency of notches in 13 of 20 individuals.
source: Serpine3cbg18 fish also showed a high frequency of notches in 13 of 20 individuals (Figure 4—source data 2, source data on Dryad).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic observations presented in Figure 4—source data 2.

claim: Eyes of both serpine3cbg17 and serpine3cbg18 individuals had a significantly reduced solidity in comparison to their WT siblings.
source: Eyes of both serpine3cbg17 and serpine3cbg18 individuals had a significantly reduced solidity in comparison to their WT siblings (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p=0.009 and p=6.35e-9, respectively, Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of eye shape presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Iris circularity is significantly reduced in homozygous individuals of both serpine3cbg17 and serpine3cbg18 lines.
source: Iris circularity, another descriptor of the eye shape deviation, is also significantly reduced in homozygous individuals of both lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mutations in serpine3 cause eye shape deviations in zebrafish.
source: Together this indicates that mutations in serpine3 cause eye shape deviations in zebrafish.
evidence: The claim is supported by the consistent phenotypes observed in two independent knockout lines.

claim: The distance between retina and lens is reduced in homozygous fish of both serpine3cbg17 and serpine3cbg18 alleles.
source: While ocular structure and optic nerves of all inspected eyes are largely normal (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), the distance between retina and lens is reduced in homozygous fish of both alleles (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis presented in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: All retinal layers were present in the mutant retinae, but they are generally less organized and structured compared to WT siblings.
source: A detailed inspection of the retinal organization revealed that although all retinal layers were present, the mutant retinae are generally less organized and structured compared to WT siblings.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis presented in Figure 4F.

claim: Retinal cells appear reduced in number and less densely packed in serpine3 knockout fish.
source: Retinal cells appear reduced in number and less densely packed.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological observations presented in Figure 4F.

claim: Rod outer segments and the pigmented RPE cells were not clearly separated in homozygous fish of both alleles.
source: Most prominently, we noticed that rod outer segments and the pigmented RPE cells, which were aligned in WT fish, were not clearly separated in homozygous fish of both alleles (Figure 4Fc-e, Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis presented in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Large clusters of pigmented cells were observed in the photoreceptor layer of serpine3 knockout fish.
source: Furthermore, we observed large clusters of pigmented cells in the photoreceptor layer (empty arrows, Figure 4Fc-e) as well as single displaced pigmented cells in all retinal layers (yellow arrows, Figure 4Fc-e).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis presented in Figure 4F.

claim: Single displaced pigmented cells were observed in all retinal layers of serpine3 knockout fish.
source: Furthermore, we observed large clusters of pigmented cells in the photoreceptor layer (empty arrows, Figure 4Fc-e) as well as single displaced pigmented cells in all retinal layers (yellow arrows, Figure 4Fc-e).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis presented in Figure 4F.

claim: KO of serpine3 in zebrafish results in morphological defects in the eye, characterized by differences in eye shape and retinal organization.
source: This shows that KO of serpine3 in zebrafish results in morphological defects in the eye, characterized by differences in eye shape and retinal organization.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined histological and phenotypic observations.

claim: rs1028727 is located ~10 kb upstream of the SERPINE3 transcription start site and is associated with a decreased area of the optic nerve head.
source: rs1028727 is located ~10 kb upstream of the SERPINE3 transcription start site and is associated with a decreased area of the optic nerve head (Bonnemaijer et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by GWAS data analysis and a citation to Bonnemaijer et al., 2019, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: rs7327381 is located ~97 kb downstream of the SERPINE3 transcription start site and is associated with an increase in corneal curvature.
source: rs7327381 is located ~97 kb downstream of the SERPINE3 transcription start site and is associated with an increase in corneal curvature (Fan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by GWAS data analysis and a citation to Fan et al., 2020, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Human SNPs linked to SERPINE3 are associated with eye phenotypes, supporting a putative ocular function of human SERPINE3.
source: This suggests that human SNPs linked to SERPINE3 are associated with eye phenotypes, supporting a putative ocular function of human SERPINE3.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the GWAS data analysis.

claim: Müller glia are the major retinal macroglia and perform numerous functions.
source: MG are the major retinal macroglia and perform numerous functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about Müller glia.

claim: Müller glia maintain the blood-retinal barrier and regulate vascularization by removing waste products and secreting (neuro)trophic substances and signaling molecules.
source: By removing waste products and secreting (neuro)trophic substances and signaling molecules, they maintain the blood-retinal barrier and regulate vascularization (Reichenbach and Bringmann, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reichenbach and Bringmann, 2013.

claim: Müller glia are essential for the long-term viability of photoreceptors and other neuronal cell types.
source: Most importantly, MGs are essential for the long-term viability of photoreceptors and other neuronal cell types (Bringmann et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bringmann et al., 2009.

claim: The serpine3 KO fish phenotype resembles those previously observed in experiments that perturb MG function.
source: Our serpine3 KO fish exhibit a disorganization of RPE cells, a phenotype that resembles those previously observed in experiments that perturb MG function.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous studies.

claim: Selective ablation of MG in adult mice results in eye defects including aggregation of RPE cells and displacement of pigment granules in the ganglion cell layer.
source: For example, selective ablation of MG in adult mice results in eye defects including aggregation of RPE cells and displacement of pigment granules in the ganglion cell layer (Shen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shen et al., 2012.

claim: Müller glia span the entire retina, connecting the extracellular space of retinal neurons, the vitreous and the capillaries at the apical retina.
source: However, MG span the entire retina, connecting the extracellular space of retinal neurons, the vitreous and the capillaries at the apical retina (Reichenbach and Bringmann, 2013; Klimczak et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Reichenbach and Bringmann, 2013 and Klimczak et al., 2009.

claim: A secreted protein from Müller glia may affect other eye subtissues.
source: It is therefore possible that a secreted protein, as predicted for serpine3 based on its conserved signal peptide, may also affect other eye subtissues.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from MG anatomy and serpine3's predicted secretion.

claim: In zebrafish, MG are able to regenerate retinal neurons upon injury.
source: Finally, in zebrafish, MG are able to regenerate retinal neurons upon injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about zebrafish retinal regeneration.

claim: Serpine3 does not seem to be involved in stress-induced regeneration as it is upregulated in resting MG that do not proliferate.
source: However, serpine3 does not seem to be involved in this process as during stress-induced regeneration, it is upregulated in resting MG that do not proliferate (Hoang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hoang et al., 2020.

claim: In mouse and human, SERPINE3 seems to be expressed in RPE.
source: While our experiments in zebrafish show serpine3 expression in MG, which is in agreement with Hoang et al., 2020, in mouse and human, SERPINE3 seems to be expressed in RPE (Hoang et al., 2020; Hadziahmetovic et al., 2012; Cowan et al., 2020) indicating that cell type specificity may differ between mammals and fish.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hoang et al., 2020; Hadziahmetovic et al., 2012; Cowan et al., 2020.

claim: Cell type specificity of SERPINE3 expression may differ between mammals and fish.
source: While our experiments in zebrafish show serpine3 expression in MG, which is in agreement with Hoang et al., 2020, in mouse and human, SERPINE3 seems to be expressed in RPE (Hoang et al., 2020; Hadziahmetovic et al., 2012; Cowan et al., 2020) indicating that cell type specificity may differ between mammals and fish.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the comparison of expression patterns across species.

claim: SERPINE3 may have a similar function in mammals and zebrafish despite secretion by different cell types, as it is likely a secreted extracellular protein.
source: As SERPINE3 is likely a secreted extracellular protein, it is possible that it has a similar function in mammals and zebrafish, despite secretion by different cell types.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from the predicted secretion of SERPINE3.

claim: SERPINE3 is upregulated in human patients with age-related macular degeneration.
source: SERPINE3 is upregulated in human patients with age-related macular degeneration (Newman et al., 2012), a progressive eye disease that is linked to chronic inflammation and wound healing.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Newman et al., 2012.

claim: Age-related macular degeneration is a progressive eye disease that is linked to chronic inflammation and wound healing.
source: SERPINE3 is upregulated in human patients with age-related macular degeneration (Newman et al., 2012), a progressive eye disease that is linked to chronic inflammation and wound healing.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about age-related macular degeneration.

claim: Mouse Serpine3 is upregulated after experimental overexpression of neurotrophin-4, a neuroprotective factor that promotes retinal survival.
source: Consistent with a role in retinal survival, mouse Serpine3 is upregulated after experimental overexpression of neurotrophin-4, a neuroprotective factor that promotes retinal survival (Machalińska et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Machalińska et al., 2013.

claim: SERPINE3 is a hallmark gene of differentiated, healthy human RPE cells.
source: Furthermore, SERPINE3 is a hallmark gene of differentiated, healthy human RPE cells (Radeke et al., 2015; Boles et al., 2020; Sripathi et al., 2021) that also have neurotrophic functions in the retina.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Radeke et al., 2015; Boles et al., 2020; Sripathi et al., 2021.

claim: Human RPE cells have neurotrophic functions in the retina.
source: Furthermore, SERPINE3 is a hallmark gene of differentiated, healthy human RPE cells (Radeke et al., 2015; Boles et al., 2020; Sripathi et al., 2021) that also have neurotrophic functions in the retina.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about RPE cells.

claim: Perturbation of proper SERPINE3 expression or function may influence age-related diseases or human eye phenotypes.
source: It is thus conceivable that perturbation of proper SERPINE3 expression or function may influence age-related diseases or human eye phenotypes, as indicated by human polymorphisms that are linked to SERPINE3.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from the expression patterns and GWAS data.

claim: The LACTBL1 gene encodes a putative serine proteinase.
source: The LACTBL1 gene encodes a putative serine proteinase (Liobikas et al., 2006) and has an expression pattern similar to retina phototransduction genes (Uhlen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liobikas et al., 2006.

claim: LACTBL1 has an expression pattern similar to retina phototransduction genes.
source: The LACTBL1 gene encodes a putative serine proteinase (Liobikas et al., 2006) and has an expression pattern similar to retina phototransduction genes (Uhlen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Uhlen et al., 2010.

claim: 20 kb upstream of LACTBL1 is a linked SNP (rs10158878) that is associated with refractive error in human.
source: Furthermore, 20 kb upstream of LACTBL1 is a linked SNP (rs10158878) that is associated with refractive error in human (GWAS catalog, Hysi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by GWAS data and a citation to Hysi et al., 2020.

claim: A missense mutation (rs6905572) within SAPCD1 is associated with macular degeneration.
source: Another uncharacterized candidate gene with a strong visual acuity associated loss pattern is SAPCD1. A missense mutation (rs6905572) within SAPCD1 is associated with macular degeneration (dbSNP, Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by dbSNP data and a citation to Chen et al., 2010.

claim: The LRIT2 gene is linked to SNPs (rs12217769 and rs745480) that are associated with macular thickness and refractive error in human.
source: The LRIT2 gene is linked to SNPs (rs12217769 and rs745480) that are associated with macular thickness and refractive error in human.
evidence: The claim is supported by GWAS data analysis.

claim: Lrit2 knockdown in zebrafish led to a reduction in eye size.
source: Whereas this gene was not functionally characterized at the time our screen was conducted, a recent study showed that lrit2 knockdown in zebrafish led to a reduction in eye size (Chiang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chiang et al., 2020.

claim: A high-throughput screen in mouse found that Pkd1l2 KO leads to abnormalities in lens morphology.
source: Finally, a high-throughput screen in mouse found that Pkd1l2 KO leads to abnormalities in lens morphology (Dickinson et al., 2016), but no follow-up experiments exist.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dickinson et al., 2016.

claim: An intronic SNP (rs873693) in PKD1L2 is associated with age onset of myopia.
source: A potential role of this gene in human disease is also indicated by an intronic SNP (rs873693), which is associated with age onset of myopia (GWAS catalog, Hysi et al., 2020; Tedja et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by GWAS data and citations to Hysi et al., 2020 and Tedja et al., 2018.
